speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement concerning the implementation of the report of the royal commission on coal.
Hon. members who have carefully read the report of the royal commission on coal know what a complex document it is. They know how intensively its information, implications, proposals and recommendations must be studied, in relation to existing provisions and assistance for coal, before appropriate decisions can be reached on the practicality of certain of the report's recommendations. In short, the Rand report is the type of public document which demands the most serious study from each of us. It is also the type of document which demands the most serious, systematic and meticulous study by the government.
I can inform you that such a study by the government is in progress. It is occupying the attention of an interdepartmental committee consisting of senior officers of the Department of Finance, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Labour, the privy council office, the national energy board and the dominion coal board, under the chairmanship of a senior officer of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
The committee has been given clear and specific instructions. It is "to study and report to the cabinet on the recommendations of the royal commission on coal relating to subsidies and research" and on such representations as have been received by the government.
While such a thorough evaluation of the Rand report is in progress, hon. members will not, I think, expect me to have formed final opinions regarding its recommendations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Has the minister any supplementary information he can give the house in regard to the very serious incident which occurred at the officers' mess at Leopoldville in the Congo on Monday night?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INCIDENT AT LEOPOLDVILLE
speechtext:
I have had some telegrams in connection with the situation there. Perhaps I can summarize it in this way.
On Monday night at approximately 7.45 p.m. a force of Congolese troops attacked the Ghana embassy in Leopoldville. The Canadian signal corps officers' mess, which is some 250 yards away from the embassy, was hit by small arms fire and at least two shells from 37 millimetre guns. The firing was heavy for approximately three hours and sporadic for the balance of the night.
Canadian personnel of the 57th signal unit are billeted in the Athenee Royal building 500 yards from the Ghana embassy. That building was not attacked directly although some officers moving from the mess were fired upon. I am very glad to be able to report to the house that there were no Canadian casualties as a result of this incident. The situation remains tense and the Canadian signals personnel, including officers as well as men, are remaining in the Athenee Royal. This building was formerly a boys' school and houses the Canadian signal establishment in Leopoldville, including the tape relay centre and the main radio transmitter, thus they will be able to continue in operation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Does the abstention yesterday by the Canadian delegation from the vote to seat the Congolese delegation at the United Nations mean that the Canadian government no longer recognizes Joseph Kasavubu as president of the Congolese republic?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONGO'-CANADIAN ABSTENTION FROM VOTE ON DELEGATION
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The abstention yesterday by the representatives of Canada at the United Nations means that we are following our policy of deciding what we think is the best policy for Canada and
Inquiries of the Ministry voting and acting accordingly, regardless of what influence may be brought to bear on us by other countries.
The position in this particular case is that Canada is one of the three European and North American countries having troops in the Congo, the other two being Sweden and Ireland. I think there are 18 contingents altogether and the remaining 15 are from Asia and Africa. Each of these 18 countries has a representative on what is called the advisory committee on the Congo, which has been meeting quite frequently and dealing with the problems that arise in connection with the United Nations forces in the Congo.
Until yesterday no one had been seated to represent the Congo at the United Nations, and in view of our having troops there and being on this committee we decided that we would not participate in the disputes with respect to who should represent the Congo in the United Nations. That is the reason we abstained yesterday, and we have also abstained on earlier motions. We abstained on a vote brought about by the countries which were anxious to seat representatives of Prime Minister Lumumba.
That is all that should be taken from the vote yesterday. Sweden and Ireland also abstained, and I think all but a handful of the African and Asian countries which are on this committee and have forces in the Congo also abstained.

I have made inquiries and am advised that the condition of this lighthouse, which, as the hon. member knows, is of wooden construction, is such that it cannot be repaired nor can it be moved. I am sorry to say, Mr. Speaker, that on account of the very substantial difference in cost the department feels it must proceed with the construction of the steel type of lighthouse.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister a question based on a recognition of priorities at this time, with government business before this house. In view of the paramount importance of issues which are now before the fifteenth session of the general assembly of the United Nations, and the international picture, is consideration being given to the earliest possible opportunity for a discussion on the Congo and international policy matters?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):

Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman as to the need of a full discussion on the international situation at the earliest possible date. There are many problems which face us today on which it would be most helpful to have the views of parliament.


This is also another matter that will be of interest to all hon. members. I expect shortly to be able to announce the date of the prime ministers' conference to be held in London, at which matters of signal importance to the commonwealth will arise and in respect of which the views of hon. members as to the attitude which they take to these problems would be most helpful. Subject to an arrangement being made between those who are in charge of the processes of the house in order to have the house operate efficiently and constructively, I will do everything I can to expedite an early discussion on these very important matters.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 22, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Walker-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954, to further encourage the demand for housing by increasing the loan ratios and extending the periods of repayment for loans made to home owners and home builders and for rental housing; to increase from $25 million to $50 million the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for urban redevelopment purposes; to increase from $200 million to $500 million the amount of home improvement loans that may be guaranteed under part IV of the act by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; to authorize the corporation to undertake jointly with provincial governments and municipalities the acquisition, improvement and conversion of existing buildings in urban renewal areas for housing purposes; to authorize the corporation to make loans to universities to assist in the construction of residential accommodation for students; to authorize the corporation to make loans and rebates thereon to municipalities or other competent municipal authorities to assist in the construction of sewage projects for the elimination of pollution and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last night I was discussing the desirability of providing houses for Canadian people at prices within their reach. On reading through the resolution and the remarks of the minister introducing it, I note that there are six very important provisions which are to be included in the proposed amendments.
One of these is the increase in the loan ratio, which is proposed to be increased from 90 per cent of the appraised lending value of the home to 95 per cent of the appraised lending value. This will have the effect of decreasing the down payment very considerably. It will now be possible for home owners to purchase a home-providing the sale price is in reasonable relation to the

appraised lending value-with a valuation of from $12,000 to $14,000 with a down payment of $600. With the previous loan ratio of 90 per cent of the appraised lending value of such a home the down payment would be $1,200.
Another measure taken to make it easier for people of limited income to purchase and pay for homes are the mortgage repayment terms, which are proposed to be extended from 30 to 35 years. It is estimated that on a $12,000 home this additional time given in connection with the mortgage repayments will decrease the monthly payment by approximately $3.50.
There is one other point in connection with these proposed amendments that I would like to briefly discuss. This concerns the interest rate charged. To be sure that what I have to say is correct I would like to refer to the minister's statement of yesterday, on page 91 of Hansard, where he was discussing this matter of the interest rate. The minister used these words:
It has been suggested by some that demand could be stimulated-
That is, the demand for houses.
-by a lowering of the interest rate as well.
There he is referring to these other proposed provisions in the amendment.
So it could, but in the present market a lower interest rate would reduce the amount of private lending under the act, and place heavier pressure on the federal government to meet the increased demand for loans. Even today, with the moderation in the pressure of demand which I have already mentioned, the federal government through C.M.H.C. is still carrying a large part of the lending load and hon. members will keep in mind that we are just residual lenders; we make no direct loans unless the borrower has been refused by a bank or by another approved lender. It is no part of our intention to increase the demand for housing funds and at the same time kill the incentive of private lenders to supply as much of the funds as possible. Again I cannot forget the way in which the funds dried up toward the end of 1959, when an interest rate of 6 per cent became totally unrealistic and when the borrowers turned in droves and in the thousands to the government to help them out of their dilemma.
I can fully appreciate the import of those words and the reasoning behind them. I believe it was necessary in 1959 to raise the interest rate on these housing loans, and I am quite willing to accept the minister's contention on behalf of the government that it is necessary to continue the present interest rate of 6J per cent. However, I am assured that this matter is kept under constant review, and I urge upon the minister and the government the desirability of lowering the interest rates on housing loans just as soon as conditions in the money market make this practicable.
National Housing Act

I cannot but be impressed by the magnitude and scope of the undertaking which the Minister of Public Works has envisaged in the resolution which has been placed before us for consideration. I am quite sure-and I say this having had an opportunity of reading some of the press comments-that this will stimulate the imagination and advance the thinking of people in Canada. I think this is more than indicated by the attitude taken by the opposition. We hear sometimes of damning with faint praise, but the attitude of the opposition has, on the contrary, been that of praising with faint and feeble damns.
The scope of the various items in the proposed legislation which have been incorporated in this resolution has left the official opposition breathless. I have no doubt that such a resolution would have taken them years to conceive and many more years to bring before parliament. As the hon. member who has just resumed his seat pointed out, there are six separate and definite items contained in this resolution. Each of them would, in itself, amount to a tremendous undertaking. When put together in one resolution they will do a great deal for the economy of Canada.
I had the opportunity yesterday of hearing the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who generally, I think, approved the principles contained in this resolution. However, I did not quite understand what he was driving at when he said, as reported at page 100 of Hansard:
I should like to pose the problem to him which this represents to a person over 30 years of age. In most plants in Canada the normal retirement age is 65. I am afraid that a large number of people who have been eligible under the old arrangement and who are past the age of 30 will now become ineligible because, as the minister knows, very many people are just on the borderline of being eligible.
It seems to me that is not a valid criticism. The question of eligibility is based on factors which apply at the time the application is actually made. However, before coming to that part of his contribution the hon. member did say something on which I intend to enlarge briefly. As reported at page 90, he referred to the pricing of lots in outlying areas close to metropolitan centres. I think I can do no better here than to read a brief quotation from Time magazine which appeared in the Canadian edition of August 29, 1960. I endorse and adopt the language and phrasing as well as the thoughts behind this quotation. This article begins on page 58; it is entitled "The Costly Earth" and says:
The man who faces inflation's crudest bite is the U.S. home builder who starts off in search of land for his dream house.

National Housing Act
I might paraphrase here and say "The Canadian home builder" because this applies equally to Canada.
Since 1950 the price of U.S. land for home building has soared anywhere from 100 per cent to 3,760 per cent-while building material prices have climbed a less spectacular 24 per cent and building trade wages 60 per cent.
In parts of Miami, land worth $500 an acre ten years ago sells for $7,500 ... Result: the family that wants to build in the suburbs now has to pay 19 per cent of a house's total cost for a far-out piece of land v. 12 per cent on a similar house in 1950 for land much closer to the city.
I have had some personal experience of that situation and I suggest that those figures are very moderate. After I came back from overseas in 1945 1 built a house near a large centre, in 1946 and 1947, and the percentage which the value of the land bore to the total cost of the house was approximately 6 per cent. Not more than two years ago, when I was interested in acquiring another property, I discovered that I was paying 18 or 19 per cent of the total cost for the land alone, just as is suggested in the article from which I have read. This process, if it continues, may have very serious consequences.
I continue to quote from this article, which is a citation from House & Home, a United States periodical:
In city and suburb alike, says House & Home, the present tax structure harnesses the profit motive backward; it abets speculation, penalizes development. Underdeveloped land and vacant city lots are taxed, on the average, at less than 25 per cent valuation across the U.S. v. 40.8 per cent for business properties. Land, comprising one third of the U.S. national wealth, carries less than 5 per cent of the total tax load. Not suprisingly, land speculation has made more millionaires since world war II than any other form of U.S. business or investment.
This refers, of course, to the United States but it could equally be applicable to this country.
If the U.S. is to avoid an even bigger land bust than in the '20's, concludes House & Home, cities and towns must act fast. Most experts agree that the first point of attack should be to ease the too-heavy tax burden on houses and other improvements, multiply the too-easy tax load on unimproved land, and make the unearned increment in land prices provide much more of the taxes needed to provide the streets, water, sewers and schools without which unimproved land would be neither livable nor saleable.
I hasten to add, of course, that according to the division of constitutional responsibility in this country as between the dominion and provincial governments this is a matter which lies within the exclusive jurisdiction and competence of the provinces, though it has been delegated in many cases to municipal corporations. However, when we consider the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been spent under our housing legislation since
[Mr. Baldwin.1
it was first placed on the statute books, we can only reach the conclusion that much of it has been, in fact, sterile.
Today one laudable purpose of this legislation is to further stimulate and expand the building trades and the plants which produce the material required for building houses. It is a matter of some concern that on the basis of present figures approximately 20 per cent of the moneys that will be expended will go toward the price of lots rather than being used for other more useful purposes. I realize that the minister is powerless to do anything about this in so far as this legislation is concerned, but I do suggest to the minister in furtherance of this very worth-while objective that he might consider the possibility at some time of extending regulations so that where it appears that the cost of the lots and the land on which these houses are to be erected constitutes a far larger percentage of the price than is proper those properties will not be eligible for benefits under this legislation. I merely throw out this thought and possibly it may be explored at a later date in conferences with municipal and provincial authorities.
I wish to offer one further constructive suggestion and indeed, this resolution is deserving of nothing but constructive suggestions. When the hon. member for Cariboo participated in this debate yesterday he referred to the great volume of construction which is likely to take place in his area. 1 have the honour to be the representative of the constituency which adjoins his on the Alberta side of the border. The benefits of legislation of the nature of that under discussion were not made available to these more remote areas as early as they were to other parts of the country. That has resulted in situations in previous years where in the larger metropolitan centres there were sometimes surpluses of houses which could not be disposed of readily whereas in parts of the country like that which I represent it proved almost impossible to keep abreast of the demand.
I am prompted to mention this because of the reference in the speech from the throne to the fact that a western route through my own part of the country is proposed for the construction of the railway to Great Slave lake. I can easily pinpoint approximately 18 or 20 towns or villages which will come into existence in this area. These places will urgently need the benefits of legislation of this kind. It might well be that in the future the minister, having regard to his responsibilities under the administration of the National Housing Act, in spite of the fact that some areas of the country are not in as great need for funds for house building, will

deem it necessary to extend by regulation the benefits available under this legislation to districts such as mine which in the past have not received the same degree of attention that has been received by more central and metropolitan areas.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to intervene but briefly in the debate. There are a good number of items in the resolution concerning which one could offer congratulations and special thanks to the minister but I intend to limit myself to two developments that are of particular interest to the area I represent, an area which in some 20 years has more than doubled its population. I think that recent visitors to Halifax would have to agree that it is almost unrecognizable today compared with its previous condition which perhaps might have been characterized by some as a bleak city shrouded in its role of east coast Atlantic port.
For one thing, the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area is one of the great centres of university learning in Canada. We have at least six universities there. All of them have expanded greatly in recent years. I do not intend at this time to enter into a debate on the perennial problem arising from the fact that Nova Scotia has more university students per capita than any other part of Canada but I do wish to say that we in Halifax will be in the forefront of those universities racing to be the first to take advantage of the amendment to the act which will soon be placed before us under which assistance will be made available for the construction of university residences. I think the University of King's College, the oldest English speaking institution of learning in Canada at the university level will achieve that honour or at least with some pardonable pride, I hope so, because recently that university gave me the honour of asking me to be a member of its board of governors. This decision will be taken, I assume, almost simultaneously with the passage by the House of Commons of those amendments to the legislation which will explain the benefits of long term low interest loans to the universities of this country.
King's College has been somewhat fettered by a lack of space and finances. Those associated with the university are ambitious as are all other Halifax universities. It is our proud hope very shortly to open the first Latin American institute in Canada and so provide to students from Central and South America facilities for university life in a Canadian city. It is our feeling that this can best be accomplished by having students from other countries pursue university life fully as can be done better by having them established in residences rather than simply
National Housing Act
scattered about in houses nearby. The realization of that dream would, I daresay, be virtually impossible without more residential space. King's College has room for less than 200 students in its present residence. The minister's proposal when accepted and adopted by us in parliament will mean a fine new building there. It will do more than alleviate the problem of providing residences for Canadian university students but will enable us in Halifax to bid a very warm welcome to students from the southern part of this hemisphere.
The other point I wish to make is that our area has been a rapidly expanding one. On January 1, we welcome yet another city to Canada. The town of Dartmouth will become a city more than double its previous size and almost double its previous population. It will meet numerous problems in relation to municipal services. Those portions of the minister's proposal concerning main and trunk sewerage, while they deal with a rather mundane thing, still give one cause to rejoice.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to let this opportunity slip by without telling the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) how grateful I am to him for the significant resolution he submitted to the house, nor without mentioning the benefits this resolution holds in store for the Canadian people, and more particularly for those I represent in this house.
I represent an essentially industrial constituency. My constituents will therefore welcome this resolution with much joy and satisfaction as it will, first of all in the social field, give them the opportunity of solving the housing problem and further, of solving or allaying the unemployment problem.
I have been a practicing medical doctor for more than 38 years in the great riding of Quebec West, with as I just said an essentially working population composed of families who, as it was customary in those days, succeeded in becoming home owners on their small family earnings. At that time, there was no social legislation to assist them, but they nevertheless brought up large families, in housing accommodation that was often too small, and succeeded in living in relative comfort. I was living with them through that difficult period. With our present social legislation, and the expansion and development that have taken place in our society, the living standard of my fellow citizens has been increased and those people are now entitled, just like anybody else, to a better standard of living, not to mention the fact that the premises in which they lived at that time have now become inadequate and for a great many of them turned into slums.

National Housing Act
More than 22 years ago, the government in power at the time, with its pretention of having succeeded in all fields, used to send us back the same candidate every four years to solicit our votes; we saw him on those occasions but we would not see him again for four more years. Housing was never a problem, except in the last few years. So when my constituents did me the honour of choosing me as their representative in the nation's government, I immediately made it a point to meet the then minister of public works (Mr. Green) to inform him of housing conditions in my constituency. The minister was kind enough to look into the problem and try to improve our really deplorable housing situation. He therefore lent his support to the first instalment on a 500 unit low cost housing development, of which 160 houses were to be built in 1958. The houses were built in 1958 and were immediately occupied, because the rents were in line with the means of the working people, and then it was a matter of keeping up the good work.
On a number of occasions, I also tested the patience of the present Minister of Public Works, and I hope he will forgive me for perhaps taxing his patience to the limit at times. However, I had faith in him, and kept pressing until the day when, a month ago, the Minister of Public Works asked me to announce that he had authorized a $965,000 loan for the building of 102 houses, in this case single family units, for the welfare of workers in my constituency.
I therefore wish to thank the minister and his colleague for rendering a great service to the working class in allowing the promoters of this first 500 house development to build, in this case, 102 units on which, the work,
I have been promised, will start very shortly, as a means of fighting winter unemployment. The promoters of the project have promised me that the work will be starting within two weeks, to the satisfaction of all concerned. Again I thank the Minister of Public Works for authorizing this project.
I would not resume my seat without saying a few words about the advantages of this measure in connection with the accommodation of our university students and as far as I am concerned, more particularly those of Laval University, of Quebec, the oldest and one of the largest of this country, for its students face a housing problem.
I am sure that this measure will rank among the best ever put forward by a gov-

ernment, since it is one of the most human, not to say the most social one ever put forward in this country to encourage and help education, to alleviate the unemployment problem and to improve living conditions.
I therefore thank the Minister of Public Works and I am happy to express to him the gratitude of those who will benefit by this measure.
