Mr. Chairman, there are a few remarks I should like to make at this stage of the discussion. First of all, I wish to say that in my estimation the minister should be commended on the majority of the recommendations which he is putting forward at this time. I believe they are forward looking and will prove of great benefit, if not in the immediate future, at least in the long run in the Dominion of Canada.
I am not one of those who believes that because he is in opposition he should always criticize. I believe that the commendation which is due should be given. I do believe that advanced steps are being made in many ways according to the explanation that has been given by the minister as to the purport of this resolution and the legislation that is to follow.
However, there is one phase on which I should like to comment, and if I misunderstand it I hope the minister will correct me. My listening to the minister yesterday leads me to believe that now money will be available for housing in rural areas even though there is no sewerage system there. With that I completely agree. This means they will have to use septic tanks. However, if my understanding is correct no loans whatsoever may be made in urban areas unless they are connected to a trunk sewer. With that I do not agree. There are in Canada-I know there are in British Columbia and I know there are within a few miles of my own home in the city of Vancouver-large areas like the municipality of Burnaby with over 100,000 population, the Delta area, the Surrey area, the Coquitlam area, and so forth, which are heavily populated but which in large part have not as yet any trunk sewerage system.
I completely fail to understand why those areas under the proposed legislation should be denied the availability of loans because in particular localities in those areas there is not at the present time a sewerage system.
A septic tank is considered healthy in a rural area if it is properly installed. Why are

loans to be denied in a part of a municipality which as yet has not that type of sewerage disposal unit? From my knowledge of the lower mainland of British Columbia I can assure the minister that advantage would be taken of this proposed legislation almost immediately if he would give consideration to making what I think is the most required and necessary change.
I think the minister should also keep in mind the fact that under the building and health bylaws of cities like Vancouver and the adjoining municipalities the property owner, once a trunk sewer is installed, is given a year or two years to stop using a septic tank and have a connection made with the trunk sewer. I can speak with a great deal of knowledge of this matter because I happen to be a trustee of a large property right in the city of Vancouver which made use of a septic tank until 18 months ago. At that time a sewer system was installed on the street and as executive director of the trusteeship I was told that within 12 months we had to make a connection with the sewer.
I do not think the ultimate cost of tying into the sewer system when it is installed is going to stop anybody in Burnaby, Surrey, Delta, Coquitlam or Burquitlam, for example, from taking advantage of this legislation because at the most it would only amount to $75 or $100 one year, two years or five years from now to make the connection with the trunk sewer. Because I think this matter is of paramount importance I ask the minister to give immediate consideration to whether or not he will make that alteration in what I have already said I believe to be the most commendable proposals which he is making at this time.
There is only one other point I wish to discuss at this time. I should like to ask him to give consideration to an extension which on philosophic and logical grounds is perhaps not in tune with the views of his own party and those of private enterprise generally. I have in mind the federal government taking the initiative and entering into at least one phase of home construction. I would not make this proposal with respect to all home construction because I know I would be ramming my head against a free enterprise brick wall. However, I believe very conscientiously that there is one phase with respect to which the minister should give serious consideration to the federal government taking the initiative.
I refer to the construction of homes or apartments for senior citizens, veterans on low pensions and others in a similar category. I understand full well that, under the resolution as outlined by the minister, when the legislation is passed the federal government
National Housing Act
will be prepared-I think this is correct- to advance up to 95 per cent through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation so that the remaining cost could be no greater than 5 per cent which should not be too much of a financial obligation or responsibility. If the federal government would take the initiative in this sphere I think it would be a very good thing.
I do not wish to negate in any way the advantages with respect to general home construction which the minister hopes will come about under the proposals he is making at this time. However, after leaving the United Nations and going home for a week before coming here I was told by a number of real estate men while I was home that they had a number of brand new homes which had never been occupied and which could be purchased by paying $100 down provided the person was able to make monthly payments of $125, $135 or $140 a month. Without knowing the exact figures, I do know there are a number of homes available in Vancouver now for $100 down if the buyer can carry the payments.
There is one very great lack, however, in the lower mainland of British Columbia particularly and I presume the same thing applies across Canada. There is a lack of homes and apartments for senior citizens and veterans with low income levels. I suggest to the minister that prompt consideration should be given to providing the extra 5 per cent and the federal government initiating the construction of homes for the senior citizens, veterans and pioneers of this country.
In making this proposal one must be honest and I hope I am being honest. I recognize that if such a policy were decided upon there would immediately be a demand all across Canada for the government to move into the field and in the initiation of such projects there must be co-operation on the provincial and municipal levels. I believe that this could be done if the federal government would take the initiative and put up the money.
In the first place, as far as the government is concerned it is a sound investment because the principal and the interest on the money will be returned. On what basis can it be done so it will not be done in a helter-skelter fashion all across Canada? I should like to remind the minister of my own experience, of which he knows, with respect to the New Vista housing project which was the first such project in British Columbia and Canada and is one of the largest. In that instance the municipality made the property available at a nominal sum of $1 so that these apartments and homes could be constructed. The

National Housing Act
municipality did so for two reasons. First of all, the project was socially desirable and, second, the agreement was that they would receive all the charges, all the taxes and so on, which they have received ever since. The project operates on a paying basis and provides wonderful homes and apartments at monthly rentals ranging from $21 to a maximum of $35.
I admit I have not thought the matter out in detail but I do know that if this were done it would give an immediate boost to the construction industry. I believe it can be done if some kind of understanding can be formulated that the government will enter into this type of construction and pay all the costs on the basis that the principal and interest will be returned and the municipalities to donate the land for a nominal sum. In this way the municipality concerned would be sharing effectively in the social responsibility. At the end of 30, 35 or 40 years the federal government would get all its money back plus interest and the property would then revert to the ownership of the municipality in repayment for the granting of the land for $1 or some other nominal sum.
I believe this is an idea which should be studied and that something can be worked out which will prove most beneficial in arriving at an early solution of one of the most critical needs of our country, low rental housing for senior citizens, veterans and others on low income. Over the long run there could be no loss to the federal government and no loss to the municipality. I put that forward as a suggestion and I hope it will be given consideration by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on this resolution. First of all, I wish to commend the minister and the government for the progressive ideas found in the resolution they have introduced at this particular time. Not only does the legislation afford relief to the housing industry but it will also be a very important factor in keeping employed many of our construction workers who depend on work in the housing industry for their livelihood.
Unfortunately, I was not in the house when a spokesman for the opposition last night, in referring to this resolution, said that some of the ideas were good and that they might well be good because they were suggested by the opposition. I think he will probably recall that over the years he and I on various occasions used similar arguments directed towards the government of which he was a supporter.
I think it must be a great satisfaction to those in the opposition, as well as to us and

to the people in the country, that this government so soon after being in office undertook a project of this sort to provide adequate housing as quickly as possible for the people of this country who deserved that sort of treatment for many years and did not get it under the previous administration. We were in opposition for many years. After the official opposition are there another 20 years I am sure they will realize that some of their arguments will no doubt bear fruit.
I might remind the hon. member that while we were in opposition we were always concerned about the interests of the municipalities. He probably will recall that on more than one occasion we urged relief by the government in some way in order that housing could be furnished, but to little avail. The record speaks for itself.
There may be in some municipalities across the country a situation in which they have housing of a sort and are probably not short of housing. I am happy to say that in my city of Sarnia-and I hope the statement applies to many others-we have only 40 new homes unsold. To me this fact is extremely important. It is also important that the government know about it, and I am sure they know through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We are not overbuilt. We certainly welcome this new resolution for many reasons.
I am going to be frank and say this. I think the government could possibly have gone a little bit further. I should like to take this opportunity of commending the minister and the government for listening to the representations that have been earnestly made and I am just going to recite a couple. When the resolution was introduced concerning housing some months ago there was a limitation on earnings. There was also a limitation on the amount of the mortgage, of course. My objection at that time was that the limit on earnings was too low. In many places where we require housing the situation is as it is in Sarnia where the earnings are quite high because we have a chemical industry which employs many technicians, engineers and scientists; the earnings are beyond the average. Representation was made to the minister that the ceiling should be raised. My own opinion is that the ceiling could be eliminated, for all the effect it has, except in a physiological way, because probably there would be only 5 per cent of the whole total who would be affected by earnings over and above the present ceiling or even the former ceiling.
Then with respect to the regulation which came into effect later concerning the requirement for sewage services in order to obtain a

loan, representation was made to the minister that there were certain areas-and I referred to the area along lake Huron near Sarnia- where sewage disposal plants would be out of the question for many years. There is, you might say, only a ribbon there between the lake and the railroad where houses would be built. It would be an injustice to the property owners of that area-and a beautiful area it is-to require that they have a so-called sewage disposal system, and I am going to have something to say about that matter a little bit later. The result was that the government lifted the regulation or suspended it for some months in order to give people the opportunity to dispose their holdings.
These regulations, of course, naturally come overnight and without notice. The result of this change by the government afforded these people the opportunity to dispose of holdings. In some cases the holdings would have meant bankruptcy because they would not have been able to sell them in areas where there would never be sewage disposal plants for many years. I think the government is to be commended for its stand and for its objectivity in meeting the current situation. No other government that I have been able to learn about or read about has taken the initiative with such effect concerning a situation that required a remedy and done so in such a short time.
I welcome the increase in the amount of the loan and also the terms for repayment. I should like to say that I am primarily interested in the other feature of this resolution. In his opening remarks on this resolution- and this concerns pollution-the minister said that the Prime Minister has been vitally interested in this problem over the years. He has been vitally interested in it. Many of us who have been here in the house for the last 15 years or more recall arguments made by him and others concerning the pollution problem. In my opinion, and I think everyone will agree, this part of the resolution is going to have a greater impact on our people in Canada and on our life than is indicated on the surface of the bill because we are finally becoming pollution conscious. I think I am safe in saying that down in my area, because of our concern about oil drilling in the great lakes, we are more pollution conscious than tax conscious and certainly everybody in Canada is tax conscious. However, very few people realize the seriousness of pollution and what it can mean and has meant to this country and in fact to this world.
The municipalities are going to welcome the opportunity provided by this government to construct sewage disposal plants within their boundaries. We know that, unfortunately, many of the municipalities in this
National Housing Act
country dump their raw sewage into the nearest available area-and they are extremely fortunate if it happens to be a river or a lake-and that is the end of it so far as they are concerned. Under this proposed legislation the municipalities which otherwise could not have afforded a modern sewage disposal plant are now enabled to obtain one.
However, I am going to say this. Most of us have the idea that a sewage disposal plant takes care of sewage which comes out of our septic tanks and from our industrial waste.
I am here to state that it does not do so. We do not have in this country-and in most places the situation is the same, even in the United States-proper sewage treatment plants.
There should be sewage treatment plants, not just sewage disposal plants so that what goes out into the lake or river, as the case may be, is not injurious to anybody, even to a minor extent. These municipalities can join together and promote the financing facilities afforded them and obtain these most necessary projects. I hope the day hastens when this country at least will show some leadership, province by province, in having all the municipalities within their boundaries provided with proper sewage treatment plants.
Furthermore, it is going to provide a great deal of winter work, and that is in itself an important factor. I think it will be greatly appreciated, also, by municipalities that there is this refund aspect of this resolution. If the job is completed, we will say by May, 1963, a certain percentage-and a very healthy percentage-is refunded to the municipalities concerned. It will mean that these municipalities, having obtained the money at a much lower rate of interest, will accept this idea of the government, and I think you will see sewage disposal plants or sewage treatment plants built all across this country.
I want to say a word about the seriousness of pollution, because we take water for granted. Polluted water is a damaged resource and it cannot serve the purpose for which it was intended. It thus becomes a public expense. The changing conditions of recent years, particularly in the industrial field, have created new problems. And we must remember that the waste from these industrial fields goes through our sewage treatment or disposal plants-and they are very important.
We in Sarnia-I am speaking now of the industrial plants in that particular area- have done an outstanding and a challenging job in trying to curb pollution. The companies in the city of Sarnia have spent over $7 million of their own hard-earned money in the last seven or eight years to curb pollution

National Housing Act
from the air and from what goes into the river. I think everyone will agree that that is most commendable action.
I want to now commend the Ontario water resources commission, which has worked so diligently and persistently, because they have a terrific task before them to convince the people of any municipality that they must use their own dollars to protect their own health. They, together with the International Joint Commission, have done a terrific job for Canada, and they get very little thanks for it because they are asking people to spend their own money.
I tell the members of this committee that until the time comes when the people of this country realize that money amounts to very little if they do not have good health the problem of water pollution will be very serious. They must realize that they had better spend a little money to get rid of pollution and enjoy the life that has been allotted to them. As population rises and demands upon the nation's water supply grow, research scientists tell us these problems will multiply. The burden on water is increasing. I said in other language a minute ago-and I do not mind emphasizing it- that it is going to take a great deal of effort just to stay even with the problem, and more, if we are going to make any improvement.
People do not realize today, in our age of research and technology, that there are over 500,000 distinct chemical compounds in use in industrial production today, while some 30 years ago there were only a few hundred. These products go through our sewage disposal plants. We know that this is so, because most of us have read a good deal about pollution and about the problem that scientists and research workers have to contend with.
In addition to the numbers which have been in use, there are over 10,000 new compounds being developed in laboratories each year. The quantity of the water in the world remains constant, and it must be used over and over again. Our method of dumping sewage into our water is not only unsavory, but unsafe. It is all the more necessary, therefore, that the people of this country realize what pollution means. It is too bad that we did not have this many, many years ago; but I doubt if people would have accepted it.
Mr. Chairman, my next remarks concern the people of Ontario. Each beach from Toronto to Hamilton-playground for two million people-has been placarded at times during these past two years with "No swimming" signs. It is about time we had some

pollution control. Two years ago the growth of algae was so rank along lake Ontario that the medical officer of Halton said, "The smell brings on nausea and lack of appetite". Some people might gloss over that statement, but I think it is a very serious one.
In addition to the water pollution we have from our sewage, there is, of course, the question of oil, which is of great concern to me, so far as oil drilling in the great lakes is concerned. I think the minister knows about that very well. Hamilton bay and lake Erie are two of the world's largest and most beautiful septic tanks. Sewage and water plants are two of the most neglected public works programs today, and I am certainly one of millions of people in this country who welcome the efforts and the program of this government to eliminate that problem to a great extent. It cannot be done overnight.
We are closing the beaches this year on the St. Lawrence, in the Cornwall area, because polluted waters are endangering health. A cursory survey was made last year, and Chicago and Erie, Pennsylvania-and they are on the great lakes system-are the only two large cities enjoying the water, and those two cities have spent millions and millions of dollars for that privilege. Milwaukee was forced to close its public beaches an August 7 because of lake Michigan's polluted water. Cleveland admits a losing fight to keep its beaches, and health officials flatly discourage any bathing in lake Erie. Ninety per cent of the people of Ontario live within 50 miles of one of the great lakes, and here, because we have had no government in the past which has assisted the municipalities in overcoming this problem, we are today faced with just what I have been reciting to you-and it is a shame.
The city of Ottawa, the capital of Canada, dumps its sewage into the Ottawa river. What do they do along the St. Lawrence, at Montreal and the rest of the cities? I think a debate on this subject is going to enlighten a few people as to the problem they are facing, and they are going to face a great many more.
Unfortunately, for more than 40 years-and we all know this-fundamentally no new sewage treatment process has been developed.
I think it is about time that our governments, research workers and scientists worked on this problem. Just because it has not been done elsewhere is no reason for us not doing it now.
In the province of Ontario we do have the Ontario water resources commission, which has several water projects and several sewage disposal projects in being. They are very persistent, and thank goodness they are. They are trying to educate the people of Ontario to the fact that we cannot waste the resource

which is commonly known as water. Without water we do not get very far. Water is the most important resource there is in this world, and there are many places in this world that would give anything to be living on a drainage basin of 298,000 square miles, such as there is in the great lakes, with its water area of
90,000	square miles.
Industry cannot live without pure water nor can our economy sustain itself without industry. That is how serious the position is. This is a problem of great magnitude and it must be controlled in order to safeguard the water resources of this country which should be regarded as the foremost economic factor in our national welfare.
The minister and the government are to be commended for their 1960 approach to a 1900 or 1850 problem. The senior government has now given a lead in this program for pollution control through its assistance to the municipalities. It is going to be appreciated. I think the municipalities will consider this resolution to be so much to their benefit that there will be very few who can afford not to come into it. It is timely and I think, also, it will be supported not only by the municipalities throughout the country but by industry and by the people of Canada generally, because water is more important to the people of this country than any other natural resource we have. There will be public support for this measure as well as private support. The financing program set out by the federal government is one which should commend itself not only to every member of this house but to all the people of Canada. I say to the minister and to the government: you have done an excellent job.

I was very interested in the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Lambton West, because this question of pollution is certainly of interest to my city, the city of Vancouver, and the provisions in this resolution which will aid in the control of pollution are of tremendous interest to me.
Our beaches are in the same mess as the hon. member for Lambton West said the beaches along lake Ontario are, but in addition we have a major fishing industry, and pollution presents an imminent danger to our runs of salmon. The city of Vancouver and the adjoining municipalities, because this is a metropolitan matter, have spent tens of thousands of dollars in the promotion and development of an engineering scheme in connection with a central sewage disposal plant. Up to now I have considered it unfortunate that the scheme has not been started but now I consider it fortunate, because the city of Vancouver and the adjacent municipalities can now take advantage of this
National Housing Act
present measure. We shall get our sewage disposal plant and we shall have a very healthy contribution from the federal government in the form of a 25 per cent rebate of those moneys expended prior to May, 1963. As I understand the resolution, the federal government will be lending up to two thirds the cost of the project. This is a matter in connection with which we on the west coast should move very rapidly.
I was also interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I myself have always taken a deep concern in the problems of our senior citizens. Because of our milder climate we perhaps have a larger percentage of senior citizens than any other region of Canada; they come to the west coast because they want in the last years of their lives to enjoy the benefits of an area which has more to offer than any other part of Canada. However, I should like to call the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver East to the minister's statement as reported on page 92 of Hansard for November 22 in which the hon. gentleman outlines how section 36 of the act would be modified so that the federal government, working directly with the municipalities and not through any intermediary body such as a provincial government, would pay 75 per cent of the cost of rehabilitating existing housing. However-and I quote the minister's actual words:
-this only in urban renewal areas designated by agreement among participating governments. In other words, it will be a corollary to the federal-provincial plans at the present time for subsidized housing.
Shortly before making that statement the minister said:
As I have reiterated many times, we are interested primarily in the little man. If we can provide for him adequate accommodation at lower cost than new housing, so much the better.
I should like the hon. member to take particular note of that phrase "at lower cost than new housing, so much the better." The practice, as was pointed out, was for municipalities to let areas get into a blighted condition to the point where it was necessary to raze the existing buildings completely and then to start building new dwellings under the provisions of the present section 36, because there is no provision in the act for federal assistance in the rehabilitation of existing buildings. This has now been changed.
Land and land assembly is a major problem and represents a major cost in any subsidized housing project. The centres of cities are usually almost 100 per cent built up, so it is necessary to go to outlying areas in order to find land available for subsidized land development, whether it is to be apartment

National Housing Act
houses, row housing or some other form of development. But the senior citizens as a rule do not want to live on the outskirts of the city. They do not like to leave the areas where they have lived for a great part of their lives. They like to be close to the shopping centres; they like to be close to activity; they like to be near the central areas of the town.
The provision in the resolution now before us will allow for the reformation of areas which are on the downgrade but which under the previous regulations would have had to become absolute slums before action could be taken. Under the proposed regulations action can be taken to stop this cancer which spreads out and eats away at the very vitals of our cities. In co-operation with the municipalities, new housing, subsidized housing, low rental housing will be available for those people who need it.
I think this is the answer to the eloquent plea made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I agree with him that this is a problem and that it must be attacked, but I say to him that it is being attacked now in the most reasonable and logical manner.
This resolution is almost a complete speech from the throne in itself. I do not know how it can ever be accomplished within the scope of a single bill. It seems to me that several bills will be necessary because there are really six items covered in the resolution. There is the change in the loan ratio; there is the extension of the period of repayment under the National Housing Act. I believe that these changes will make it much easier to raise the money necessary to build a house. The minister announced yesterday that the ratio of loan is changed from 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value to 95 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value; that the 70 per cent of the remainder continues as it was; and that the period of repayment has been extended from 30 to 35 years.
One major result of this will be to meet a complaint we have often heard in this chamber concerning what steps can be taken to stop the fantastic charges involved in house building when you consider what is paid for a second mortgage not only in terms of interest but in terms of the discount on the value of the money you are supposed to receive. You may require $3,000 and you may receive $2,000 and you pay 10 per cent on the $3,000, and things of that nature. I know scores of young people who have stretched their credit to the limit to get together all the money they could but a first mortgage was not sufficient and they had to get the balance through a second mortgage. These second mortgages are in many cases examples of usury of the worst

character. The hon. member for Nipissing held forth on this subject in his remarks.
This change as I see it will put an end to second mortgages on houses built under N.H.A. There will be no need for second mortgages because the changes in the lending ratio and in the period of repayment will bring the provisions of the legislation within the reach of practically everybody who is genuinely in the position to take on the responsibility of building a home.
The taller hon. member for Halifax during the course of his remarks expressed the thought that King's College may be the first university in Canada to take advantage of the provisions under which aid will be made available for the construction of student residences. I was talking to the president of the University of British Columbia, Dr. Norman MacKenzie, at noon today. I believe that King's College will have to move very quickly if it wishes to get ahead of the University of British Columbia in taking action in this regard. Dr. MacKenzie believes that this assistance will be of great value to his university. I know of the need for new residences at that university which has seen a fantastic growth in enrolment during the last eight years as has been the case with almost every university in Canada.
This aid is a major point in this resolution and one for which the government will receive commendation from every side of the committee. I do not wish to take any more time. There are six items dealt with in the resolution and I have touched upon only two. This resolution will give to the Canadian economy an even greater fillip than the resolution debated yesterday with respect to loans to small business. This resolution will extend the operations of C.M.H.C. into almost every area of construction and will result in a greatly expanded program of work. One important consideration is the application of this assistance to rental housing which I believe the minister said would bring approximately 1,500,000 homes under the banner of C.M.H.C.
In conclusion I join with the hon. member for Lambton West in saying that the minister and the government have done a good job. This resolution is certainly one of the best I have seen for many a day.

Mr. Chairman, I am not rising to repeat what was said so well by my friend the hon. member for Nipissing last night, but now that the government has had 18 of its supporters rise in their places to congratulate the minister and to say how strongly they support this resolution, I wonder if the supporters of the government would

consider co-operating with the official opposition in getting this resolution through so that the government could bring down this bill and we could see what is really in it.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat I am very anxious to see the bill brought down but it may very well be that I will not have an opportunity again to speak to the resolution before us or to the bill when it is brought before the house so I therefore now wish to avail myself of this opportunity of speaking because we have extremely urgent and pressing housing problems in the Yukon. I thought if I brought a few statements to the minister's attention he might be able to consider them in relation to extensions of the legislation which will be brought before us and in relation to other facets of the administration of C.M.H.C.
Our particular problem in the north generally and in the Yukon specifically is brought about by the substantially higher costs of construction there. It costs roughly 30 per cent to 40 per cent more to conduct any construction projects in the Yukon than it does in areas to the south. A home that could be built for $10,000 in Calgary or Toronto would cost $14,000 or more in the Yukon. A home costing $18,000 in the southern part of Canada would cost more than $24,000. It can be readily appreciated, therefore, that the maximum loan offered under C.M.H.C. is not sufficient to make it possible for the lower income groups there to take full advantage of the provisions of the N.H.A.
The remarks of the minister in introducing this resolution offer some hope that the situation in this respect will be in large part remedied because the changing of the ratio of the loan now available to applicants will result in a much lower down payment for those who wish to build under N.H.A. but it will still not close the large gap that exists in the Yukon when comparisons are made with building costs in other areas.
For instance, in the minister's remarks on November 22, as reported at page 91 of Hansard of that date, he indicated that the down payment for a house on which the lending value would be $14,000 will be reduced by $600. That does not reduce the down payment sufficiently to adequately enable the Yukon citizen to take advantage of N.H.A. building although it will certainly go a long way toward assisting.
I have noticed in the last two years, in Whitehorse particularly, that there has been a substantial advance in building programs mainly because of the changes introduced when the last amendments were made to the N.H.A. which increased the maximum loan
90205-6-9i
National Housing Act
available. This resulted in an increased number of new houses being constructed. Previously, three or four years ago, there had only been two units constructed in the whole of the Yukon under this program. This indicates the inadequacy of the N.H.A. to operate in the northern area. We think it is just as important in the north to make advances in terms of human resources as it is in terms of the development of our natural resources including minerals and the like in relation to which great strides have been taken in recent years.
A great deal of the housing in the Yukon is below acceptable health and social requirements. In large part, as I have said, this is owing to the very high cost of construction in the Yukon. Added to this fact is the additional factor that many people do not have the advantage of steady year around employment which would enable them to accumulate the capital required for the improvement of a house or the construction of a new one. Assistance at various levels of government is required if the urgent housing needs in the Yukon are to be met.
During the early years of the construction of the Alaska highway and of the Canol project the federal government was in large part responsible for the situation which we find in Whitehorse, where there are a series of very low standard and substandard houses in which people are living today. I say that because the advent of the Alaska highway and the Canol project resulted in an increase almost overnight of 800 to 1,000 per cent in that city's population. There was no adequate development or administration of lands. This condition was aggravated over the years by the complete lack of any intelligent administration in the way of acquiring land upon which individuals could construct houses. Not only did the federal government create the situation we now have and have had for years, namely one of those blights of which the minister spoke in his remarks in introducing the legislation yesterday, but we have a situation which has been consistently aided and abetted in its worsening of the conditions in the city. Today we have some 273 squatters within the municipal boundary of the city of Whitehorse unlawfully occupying crown and other lands. Within a radius of five to 10 miles of the city of Whitehorse there are some 550 of such unlawful occupiers of crown lands. This situation must be cured, and much assistance must be obtained from the federal government in curing it because they created it. I am speaking of the years from 1942 to about 1952. They were responsible for the creation of this very undesirable state of affairs.

National Housing Act
As I say, in the last two years extremely rapid strides have been made in home construction in the Yukon, due directly to the availability on a more equitable scale to the Yukon citizen of loans under the National Housing Act. These proposed changes in the National Housing Act are going to make a very great difference to house building in the Yukon. I believe that when they are combined with additional federal aid they may very well close the gap which exists between the Yukon citizen and other Canadians in the equitable application of the National Housing Act.
There are four methods by which the federal government can assist, in addition to those proposals which were set forth by the minister in introducing the resolution. The first one is to set up a fund creating what I will call a second mortgage fund. This is required because the proposals introduced by the minister, while they are indeed far-reaching, will still not enable the lower income earning group to build their own houses. The establishment of a second mortgage fund in the Yukon, to be administered, I suggest, by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, would greatly assist in closing the gap.
Second, I feel that a method by which the federal government could assist in the field of home improvement would be the establishment of a revolving fund of some $400,000 to $500,000 from which loans could be drawn to a maximum of $3,000, depending on the appraised value of the house that is to be improved, thus enabling existing house owners to improve their houses, and even to assist them in the purchase of a lot on which either to construct a new house or to move their existing house. Such a fund could also be used for the installation of sewer and water facilities both in the home and to hook up to existing facilities.
A third way in which the federal government could assist in alleviating this problem, which I say they created over the years, is to assist the communities and municipal governments in the Yukon to purchase lands, which would then be subdivided and serviced with water and sewer facilities and thus alleviate a very pressing squatter situation which is developing day by day.
The last proposal which I have to offer in the way of assisting the housing problem we face in the Yukon is the establishment of a low rental housing project certainly in the city of Whitehorse and in any other municipality or community in the Yukon which displays a need for it.
I am sure these four factors will cure-at least they will go a long way toward curing -that situation which, as I have said, was

assisted in its creation almost wholly by the federal government's maladministration during the war years, 1940 to 1945, and which has been abetted by the cumbersome and completely unworkable system of purchase of territorial lands since that time.
I should not close my remarks without saying that two years ago we were looking forward to National Housing Act building and applications were being approved. Some houses were being constructed and some speculative building was under way when last year the income restrictions were placed on loans available through the National Housing Act, and speculative loans were discontinued. There were one or two other features which, as far as we in the north were concerned, were extremely undesirable. Almost at once housing development ceased. I am happy to say that after I made representations to the minister early last spring -I just forget when I did so-those income restrictions were removed in so far as all the Canadian territory north of the 60th parallel was concerned. Immediately after this was done house building in the Whitehorse area pressed right ahead. As a result of the removal of those income restrictions I can point to some 25 new units built last summer. If this had not been done our housing progress would have come to a complete standstill.
This is the first opportunity that I have had to thank the minister for making this provision for the development of the human resources of the north. I am very pleased to say that in October last year the income restrictions were removed throughout the whole of Canada. This pointed up a certain faith in the north in so far as the development of the human resources of which I have been speaking is concerned.
I might say that when the hon. member for Vancouver East was speaking I was rather concerned about what I now believe to be a misinterpretation of the minister's remarks on the availability of funds for the development of services for urban communities. As I read the minister's remarks in Hansard of November 22, it would appear that these changes will allow urban redevelopment including the application of these funds toward the installation of sewer and water facilities. This will go a long way to assist us in our unorganized areas in the Yukon and particularly in our urban areas.
Another very valuable feature of the changes which I anticipate will come about concerns those who are employed in the civil service of Canada and are attached to the territorial civil service of the Yukon. Until a

couple of years ago the policy of the government, and it was a necessary one, was to create an attraction in the north to assist the government in their recruitment program so that they could obtain the necessary qualified personnel to take posts in the north. In order to do this one of the inducements was the provision of government owned housing which was constructed at government expense and then rented to the civil servants. As a result of the changes, some civil servants were building their own homes in the north last year and there are now six who are building in the new sub-division of Whitehorse. The expansions of the National Housing Act now being made are going to increase that number because by and large civil servants do not want to be occupying rented government homes. They want to own their own homes and if they can be put in a position to do so they want to be able to build them. Civil servants elsewhere in Canada do so and those in our northern areas want the same independence.
I am not suggesting that Whitehorse compares at all with places like Alert and Frobisher or other more isolated postings in Canada's north but in areas such as Whitehorse where there is other private housing there is no reason why civil servants should not be able to fulfil their desire to build their own homes in the same way as anyone else can.
I am very interested in seeing the application of that aspect of the legislation which has to do with the assistance which will be given toward creating new university accommodation. As most hon. members know, in the Yukon we have no university and all our students who leave high school and wish to take university training must go to the southern centres. Until now most of them have gone either to the University of British Columbia or the University of Alberta. Certainly there has been no adequate accommodation at the University of British Columbia to take care of young people who wish to go there to continue their studies. I am sure the new provision will improve the situation.
In completing my remarks may I refer to the four suggestions with respect to additional assistance to the Yukon which I have put before the minister, namely, a second mortgage fund, a revolving fund for home builders and home improvement loans, assistance in the way of purchasing land for subdivisions and servicing it with sewer and water facilities because our municipalities are not rich enough to pay for these things, and the establishment of a low rental project in any area that needs it, particularly in
National Housing Act
Whitehorse where the need is very urgent. All of these proposals have received assent in principle from the city of Whitehorse and were endorsed in the form of a resolution passed five or six days ago by the Yukon legislative council which is now in session.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks this afternoon will be brief. In the main I should like to find out from the minister, if I can, just how many jobs the government feels can be provided as a result of the suggested amendments to the National Housing Act. As I see it, the government is taking a very conservative attitude in these amendments and in its general approach. While the minister was in a position in July of this year to forecast some 125,000 housing starts or more, that forecast has now been scaled down to 110,000. In all of the government's actions in the housing field I think there is great evidence that the government has not only misjudged the general employment situation in Canada but has in fact misjudged the number of housing starts and the part that home construction would play in providing employment in Canada.
We have been in session for a few days now. We are now considering the government's second measure to deal with the unemployment emergency. The first had to do, of course, with loans for small business, and the measure before us now has to do with certain amendments to the National Housing Act which are laudable and are being supported by all members of the house. I am wondering whether the Minister of Public Works can give the house some assurance that this is not just a fleabite, that this is really going to mean the provision of many thousands of new jobs in Canada. In my view that is what the people of the country are looking to parliament for now, action to solve the whole problem of unemployment.
That is what we are doing.

I am trying to find out from the minister just how much you are doing. I am all in favour of what is being done but I think the people of Canada will not be satisfied at all if parliament takes action that merely nibbles at the problem and that even with the action that is being taken in this and other fields unemployment will continue to become worse and worse in the months that lie ahead. Therefore, before the resolution is passed I am asking the minister to be good enough to tell the committee how many additional jobs the government feels will be provided by the measure that is now before us.

National Housing Act
The Minister of Public Works has offered opinions on other occasions as to how many jobs were provided by other measures that were taken. I have in my hand the newsletter for November-December, 1960, issued by the department of economic development of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and on page 2 I find the following statement:
Several correspondents have taken exception to the statement made by the Hon. David1 J. Walker, Q.C., Minister of Public Works, in a speech in Toronto on September 12 and quoted in the October issue of the newsletter. Mr. Walker referred to the Mackenzie federal building in Toronto erected at a cost of $11 million "and provided 1,300 on-the-site jobs for workers in the building trades which lasted on an average of four months". Mr. Walker went on to say, "What an expensive way to solve unemployment! Dividing 1,300 jobs into $11 million we have $9,000 being required to provide one man with work for four months; $27,000 to provide one man with on-the-site work for one year."
And so on. I think there are more jobs involved in this expenditure than the minister would appear to indicate by his statement. However, if in the view of the minister a construction project takes such a huge sum of money to provide a few jobs, it would be extremely interesting to learn from him how many additional jobs may be provided by the worth-while amendments that have been placed before the house.
From what the government is doing, my impression is that this is the kind of thing a government would do normally, in an ordinary year in order to meet the housing needs of the Canadian people and that it is not really an all-embracing, emergency action to deal with an emergency situation. I think housing could provide a large number of jobs across this country, but if this is to be done there must be a massive attack on slum conditions in Canada.
I do not care what large city an hon. member may go into, my own experience has been that one can find block after block of buildings in which people live but which are a disgrace to Canada and should be torn down and replaced by proper and adequate buildings. If there were a serious attack on slum conditions all across this country I think the government would then be mounting a program that would have a substantial effect on the numbers of unemployed in this country. From any evidence I have seen thus far I cannot believe that the government can seriously expect that this measure and others that have been announced are in fact going to deal effectively with the extremely grave unemployment situation in Canada at this time. However, I am sure the members of

the committee would be grateful to the minister if he could give them some indication of what the government expects to accomplish with this program.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, at the risk of displeasing my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), I, as a town planner, would hate to let the opportunity slip by of commending the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) for the resolution he has submitted to the consideration of this committee for the purpose of bringing about several changes to the National Housing Act.
For once, Mr. Chairman, we have before us a bill the aim of which is to bring about an integrated and efficient solution to the problem of housing and urban renewal throughout this country. These new measures round off those which were introduced last session, by the Minister of Public Works, and all these measures, taken together, fully show the understanding he has of the housing and accommodation problem.
As the member for St. James, I shall speak on behalf of the citizens of that riding and, whether my colleague the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Bissonnette) likes it or not, I maintain that my constituency is more urban and even more of a workmen's riding than his own, as it is situated in the very heart of the Canadian metropolis. So, on behalf of the voters of the riding of St. James, I want to thank the Minister of Public Works for taking the opportunity of bringing about a more efficient solution than ever to the still acute housing problem for the small wage earner, at a time when the fight against unemployment made it possible.
I would not want, Mr. Chairman, to reiterate comments which have been made before on the proposed legislation, as provided in the resolution. I shall just give a brief summary. On the whole, the proposed provisions are the following: extension of the loan repayment period; increase in the ratio of the loans to the lending value rather than the building value; increase in the credit available for urban redevelopment, extension of the credit available for improvements to existing units-and I am sure that the minister said in his comments that it would comprise apartment houses; possibility of buying and using existing units in urban redevelopment areas, under a joint municipal-federal plan; possibility also of building students' residences under the limited dividend company system; and finally, a proposed solution to the sewer, sewage disposal and water pollution problem.

There is no doubt that all these measures will meet problems which are very urgent problems throughout Canada at this time. There is, first of all, the matter of helping families with a small revenue to become home owners.
The proposed provisions will help solve that problem by increasing the value of loans, decreasing the down payment, doing away with the necessity of obtaining an extremely costly second mortgage, and finally by lowering the monthly payment on the principal and interest through an extension of the loan period to 30 and 35 years.
We are dealing today with a major problem, that of making it possible for low income families to become house owners. Another problem which low income families have to face is that of renting housing units built by private industry at a cost beyond their means, although their income is too high for them to be acceptable in subsidized housing projects. The legislation now under consideration will make it possible to provide housing accommodation to those low income groups.
There is one particularly important factor here, Mr. Chairman. From the viewpoint of city planning, this is the first time that any project is put forth to help, in an absolutely efficient and practical way, to promote a municipal conservation scheme. In fact, this resolution mentions increased credit for repairs or improvements to existing houses. It will also enable municipalities to join with the federal government to purchase, improve and use existing houses for subsidized rental purposes in areas subject to urban redevelopment.
An often recurring problem is this. In certain deteriorating areas complete clearing is not allowed. This legislation however, will make it possible to clear out certain areas and open them to redevelopment. Another recurring problem is that in slum clearing you have to relocate the people living in those slums. Most of the time in our larger cities, we have to face the fact that such development is not easy and the problem then is a very complicated one.
Thanks to the proposed legislation housing units will be provided for people who are brought out of the slums. Finally, the additional amounts granted for urban redevelopment will undoubtedly speed up adequate programs throughout our cities, and it must not be overlooked that deterioration is apparent today not only in the larger cities but more and more in several smaller cities as well. I am thinking of several localities such as Anjou, St. Jean and others in
National Housing Act
the province of Quebec, near Montreal, where a redevelopment scheme is needed to modernize certain districts which were built several generations ago and are no longer adequate.
This resolution also contains a number of provisions for improved conditions in housing developments, namely the construction of low cost housing or small houses, by promoting sewer system installation and especially sewage disposal plants. This legislation will considerably help municipalities solve a problem which is found throughout Canada, that is the pollution of rivers. This legislation will be a great step forward, Mr. Chairman. It will greatly help not only in larger municipalities, but smaller ones also.
May I take this opportunity to thank the Minister of Public Works for his assistance to the city of Montreal through a recent grant of over $100,000 to be used for surveys on slum clearing and urban redevelopment possibilities. One of those surveys is more particularly concerned with slum clearing in an eastern section of the city which is located partly in the constituency of St. James and partly in that of St. Mary. It will affect about 800 families. The effect of such relocation studies will be to provide modern and sanitary homes for over 1,000 families. There is no doubt that the problem arises in many forms across Canada. Such studies will help enhance human values, as well as real estate values and will lead to a better conservation of capital invested in housing throughout Canada.
Such urban redevelopment schemes will make it possible to carry out important projects which otherwise could not have been tackled. A case in point is the slum clearance scheme in eastern Montreal, which will enable the C.B.C. to relocate its facilities in Montreal and build an integrated centre for French language radio and television broadcast, serving all of Canada. I would point out also that such programs can help small municipalities and suburbs, especially with regard to sewage disposal, and will increase the number of integrated housing development.
Before closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make two suggestions to the Minister of Public Works, the first having to do with the co-operative movement. I hope it will be possible under the regulations to be passed for the administration of the proposed act, to give maximum consideration to the co-operative movement. Housing cooperatives may have left some doubts in

National Housing Act
the past as to what they could accomplish, but I think in the last tew years, events have shown that housing co-operatives were able to do worth-while things for relatively low income families, through the savings effected by mass purchasing of materials, and also with respect to labour and to the financing of short and long term loans. One case I should like to mention here is that of a housing co-operative company in Montreal, which was set up to acquire, from the city of Montreal, a rather substantial piece of land in the northern section, upon which it will build houses that may be purchased by families with low incomes. Perhaps I should point out that the city of Montreal contributed a rather considerable amount to this scheme by selling the land to the co-operatives at a quarter of its true value. The bill now under consideration may help such developments, thus enabling some 1,000 families to live in first rate social conditions.
Mr. Chairman, I have a second suggestion, in connection with town planning. I hope that in administering the act, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will continue and indeed place greater emphasis on a commendable practice it has been following in the past. I refer to the practice, in new urban developments and in redevelopment schemes, of using the services of professional town planners wherever possible, as a means of guaranteeing first rate housing developments to our people.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote a statement made by the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, as reported in La Patrie for November 16, 1948:
We need all the houses that it Is humanly possible to build.
I am proud that this truth is being given effect by a Conservative government.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up too much time at this stage of the committee's proceedings, as it is so near the adjournment hour, but I wish to express my appreciation and support of the minister for bringing in this very important resolution.
Having served for a number of years on a municipal council I realize the importance of the present resolution to all municipalities, because it deals with housing, sewage disposal, urban renewal, and a number of other matters. I do not intend to speak on matters

that have been dealt with before, but there are one or two points that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister.
One point is in connection with the building of residences for university students. In the resolution there is provision for the building of housing accommodation for university students. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the need for residences for student nurses, graduate nurses, technicians who work in hospitals, also interning doctors.
Those who have been associated with hospital boards will realize the problem there is in finding money to erect these buildings. I would like the minister to take that matter into consideration, because in cities which have hospitals it is a very important matter and I think it is well worthy of consideration.
There is another matter in connection with sewage disposal. I think it is a very forward and a very important step that the government is taking at this time in dealing with the problem of pollution. In our part of Ontario we are very familiar with all the problems of pollution. All our beaches along lake Ontario, our rivers and canals are more or less polluted, and the municipalities have been waiting for some time for legislation of this kind to be brought forward so that they will be able to obtain the money to proceed with this work. I am glad that the Department of Public Works has taken this matter into consideration, and I hope they will make a good job of it, because in many cities and towns today they claim they have sewage disposal but they only have a very partial treatment.
In the province of Ontario-in fact, in all Canada-there should be complete sewage treatment. That means that storm sewers will have to be built and the storm water will have to be separated from the sanitary sewer. I also hope that the minister will take storm sewers into consideration when he considers the advancing of money for the building of sewers, because storm sewers are just about as important as sanitary sewers.
There is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, and that is in connection with the Ontario water resources commission. For the past two or three years the Ontario water resources commission has more or less taken over the building of sewage treatment plants in many municipalities. They find the money and build

the plants, and then they more or less rent them to the municipalities. I would be very interested to know how this new legislation would fit into a scheme of that kind, because I think it is very important that the municipalities should be in a position to obtain this rebate if they complete the work within the next two or three years, even though they do it through the Ontario water resources commission.
I have given the minister the three points which I would like him to study. These are, the matter of housing accommodation for student nurses and other hospital personnel, the matter of the Ontario water resources commission, and the matter of storm sewers, which is very important to the municipalities.
